title: Subnetting, CIDR & VLSM
summary: Master the core whiteboard skill — carving a network into subnets with CIDR notation and variable-length masks, fast and without off-by-one errors.

slides.markdown: Subnetting is the single most-practiced whiteboard exercise in networking interviews: given a block of addresses, carve it into smaller pieces that fit real teams and devices, without wasting space or breaking anything. This topic builds the mechanics up from the subnet mask to full **VLSM** planning.

**Subnetting** splits one larger network into smaller ones, each its own broadcast domain. Reasons to do it: reduce broadcast traffic on any one segment, isolate departments or security zones from each other, and allocate addresses to match actual team sizes instead of one flat block for everyone.

A company with 500 employees across five floors doesn't want one giant broadcast domain — it wants five smaller ones, each sized appropriately and independently manageable.

Finding an address's network is a bitwise **AND** between the address and the subnet mask:

![Binary AND of an address and a /26 mask, zeroing out the host bits to reveal the network address](assets/subnet-mask-anding.svg)

Every subnetting calculation — network address, broadcast address, usable range — reduces to this one operation plus knowing where the mask's 1s stop.

assets.alt: Binary AND of an address and a /26 mask, zeroing out the host bits to reveal the network address

slides.markdown:
**CIDR notation** writes the mask as a slash and a number — `/24` means "the first 24 bits are the network portion," equivalent to a mask of `255.255.255.0`. The number after the slash directly tells you two things at once: how many network bits, and by subtraction, how many host bits (32 minus the prefix).

Host bits determine subnet size: a /24 has 8 host bits → 2⁸ = 256 addresses; a /27 has 5 host bits → 2⁵ = 32 addresses. Memorizing this relationship is what makes fast subnetting possible.

Carve `192.168.1.0/24` into 4 equal subnets:

```
Need 4 subnets -> need 2 extra bits (2^2 = 4)
Original: /24 -> New prefix: /26 (24 + 2)
Each /26 subnet has 2^(32-26) = 64 addresses

Subnet 1: 192.168.1.0/26    (.0   - .63)
Subnet 2: 192.168.1.64/26   (.64  - .127)
Subnet 3: 192.168.1.128/26  (.128 - .191)
Subnet 4: 192.168.1.192/26  (.192 - .255)
```

Each block simply advances by the subnet size (64) — the block boundaries are always multiples of the subnet size, never arbitrary.

For any CIDR block, three things always follow directly from the prefix:

- **Network address** — all host bits set to 0 (the block's first address). Identifies the subnet, never assigned to a device.
- **Broadcast address** — all host bits set to 1 (the block's last address). Reserved for broadcasting to everyone on that subnet.
- **Usable host range** — everything between them.

For `192.168.1.64/26`: network = `.64`, broadcast = `.127`, usable hosts = `.65` through `.126` — 62 usable addresses out of the 64 in the block.

Fixed-length subnetting (previous example) forces every subnet to the same size — wasteful when your teams don't all need the same headcount. **VLSM (Variable-Length Subnet Masking)** lets you carve subnets of different sizes out of the same block, each sized to its actual need.

The discipline: **allocate largest-need-first**. Carve the biggest subnet off the block first, then recursively subnet what's left for the next-largest need — carving smallest-first leaves awkward, hard-to-combine fragments.

Plan `10.0.0.0/24` for subnets needing 100, 50, 20, and 10 hosts (largest first):

```
100 hosts -> need 7 host bits (2^7=128 >= 100+2) -> /25
  10.0.0.0/25       (126 usable, .1-.126)

50 hosts  -> need 6 host bits (2^6=64 >= 50+2)  -> /26
  10.0.0.128/26     (62 usable, .129-.190)

20 hosts  -> need 5 host bits (2^5=32 >= 20+2)  -> /27
  10.0.0.192/27     (30 usable, .193-.222)

10 hosts  -> need 4 host bits (2^4=16 >= 10+2)  -> /28
  10.0.0.224/28     (14 usable, .225-.238)
```

Each block starts exactly where the previous one ended, and each prefix is the smallest one that still fits (need + 2, for network and broadcast).

The reverse operation — **route summarization** (supernetting) — combines several contiguous CIDR blocks into one larger advertised route, when a router doesn't need to distinguish between them.

If you own `10.0.0.0/25` through `10.0.0.192/27` contiguously, a neighbor doesn't need four route entries — a summarized `10.0.0.0/24` covers it all in one line. This is how the global routing table stays in the hundreds of thousands of entries, not billions — see [Routing Fundamentals](routing-fundamentals).

Seeing the /24 split as a tree makes the largest-first discipline concrete:

![A /24 split via VLSM into a /25, /26, /27, and /28 sized to actual host counts](assets/vlsm-tree.svg)

A fixed-length split into four equal /26s would have wasted the majority of addresses on the 10- and 20-host subnets.

assets.alt: A /24 split via VLSM into a /25, /26, /27, and /28 sized to actual host counts

slides.markdown:
Two shortcuts make subnetting fast without a calculator:

- **Powers of two, memorized** — 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. Host count needed → round up to the next power of two → that tells you the host bits.
- **The magic number** — for the mask's last non-255 octet, `256 - <that octet>` gives you the block size (the "jump" between consecutive subnets). A `/27` has mask octet 224, magic number `256-224=32` — subnets jump by 32: `.0, .32, .64, .96...`

With these two, you can subnet on a whiteboard in seconds without touching binary at all.

| | Fixed-length subnetting | VLSM |
|---|---|---|
| Subnet sizes | All equal | Sized per actual need |
| Address efficiency | Wastes space on small subnets | Minimal waste |
| Planning complexity | Simple — one calculation | More work — allocate largest-first |
| Typical use | Uniform needs (e.g. identical branch offices) | Mixed needs (most real organizations) |

**How to decide:** if every subnet genuinely needs the same size, fixed-length is simpler to manage; the moment needs vary meaningfully, VLSM's address savings are almost always worth the extra planning.

slides.subTitle: Forgetting the network and broadcast addresses aren't usable
slides.markdown:
The single most common subnetting mistake: computing a block's total address count and forgetting that the **first (network) and last (broadcast)** addresses aren't assignable to hosts. A /27 has 32 total addresses but only **30 usable** — not 32, not 31.

When a requirement says "needs 20 hosts," you need a block with at least 22 addresses (20 + network + broadcast) — always add 2 before rounding up to the next power of two, or you'll under-provision by exactly one usable address's worth of headroom.
